Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It is known that every closed curve of length \leq 4 in R^n (n>0) can be surrounded by a sphere of radius 1, and that this is the best bound. Letting S denote the circle of circumference 4, with the arc-length metric, we here express this fact by saying that the "mapping radius" of S in R^n is 1.   Tools are developed for estimating the mapping radius of a metric space X in a metric space Y. In particular, it is shown that for X a bounded metric space, the supremum of the mapping radii of X in all convex subsets of normed metric spaces is equal to the infimum of the sup norms of all convex linear combinations of the functions d(x,-): X --> R (x\in X).   Several explicit mapping radii are calculated, and open questions noted.

outputs.L1:
It is known that every closed curve of length \(\leq 4\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (\(n>0\)) can be surrounded by a sphere of radius \(1\), and that this bound is optimal. Let \(S\) denote the circle of circumference \(4\), equipped with the arc-length metric. We express the preceding result by saying that the “mapping radius” of \(S\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is \(1\).

We develop tools for estimating the mapping radius of a metric space \(X\) in a metric space \(Y\). In particular, we show that, for a bounded metric space \(X\), the supremum of the mapping radii of \(X\) in all convex subsets of normed metric spaces equals the infimum of the supremum norms of all convex linear combinations of the functions
\[
d(x,-)\colon X\to\mathbb{R}\qquad (x\in X).
\]
We also calculate several explicit mapping radii and identify a number of open questions.
outputs.L2:
Every closed curve in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) (\(n>0\)) whose length is at most \(4\) is contained in a sphere of radius \(1\), and no smaller universal radius is possible. If \(S\) is the circle with circumference \(4\), equipped with its arc-length distance, this result can be stated by saying that the mapping radius of \(S\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) equals \(1\).

Methods are introduced for bounding the mapping radius of one metric space \(X\) in another metric space \(Y\). A principal result states that, when \(X\) is bounded, the supremum of its mapping radii over all convex subsets of normed metric spaces coincides with the infimum of the supremum norms of every convex linear combination of the distance functions
\[
d(x,-):X\to\mathbb{R},\qquad x\in X.
\]
The work also computes several mapping radii explicitly and identifies a number of unresolved problems.
outputs.L3:
Every closed curve in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) whose length is at most \(4\) is contained in a closed ball of radius \(1\). Moreover, the constant \(1\) is optimal: a curve of length \(4\), such as a circle of radius \(2/\pi\), cannot in general be enclosed in any smaller ball.

This statement can be formulated in terms of the **mapping radius**. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, the mapping radius of \(X\) in \(Y\) is the supremum, over all nonexpansive maps \(f:X\to Y\), of the smallest radius of a ball in \(Y\) containing \(f(X)\). For the circle \(S\) of circumference \(4\), equipped with its arc-length metric, the above result says that
\[
\operatorname{map\text{-}rad}(S,\mathbb{R}^n)=1.
\]

More generally, the work develops methods for estimating and computing the mapping radius of one metric space in another. These methods connect geometric containment questions with convexity and functional analysis. In particular, when \(X\) is bounded, the supremum of its mapping radii over all convex subsets of normed metric spaces admits an intrinsic description in terms of the distance functions
\[
d(x,-):X\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}.
\]
Specifically, this supremum equals
\[
\inf\left\{
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{m} c_i\,d(x_i,-)\right\|_{\infty}
:\;
m\ge 1,\quad c_i\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{m}c_i=1,\quad x_i\in X
\right\}.
\]
Thus, the relevant mapping radius can be recovered by taking the infimum of the sup norms of finite convex combinations of distance functions.

Using these tools, several mapping radii are calculated explicitly for particular metric spaces and classes of target spaces. The analysis also reveals limitations of the available techniques and leads to a number of open questions concerning exact values, optimal embeddings, and the dependence of mapping radii on the geometry of the source and target spaces.
outputs.L4:
For metric spaces \(X\) and \(Y\), the mapping radius of \(X\) in \(Y\) is defined by  
\[
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,Y)
 =\sup_{f:X\to Y\ \text{1-Lipschitz}}
   \inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{x\in X} d_Y\bigl(f(x),y\bigr).
\]
Thus, for each nonexpansive map \(f\), one takes the radius of the smallest ball in \(Y\) containing \(f(X)\), and then maximizes this radius over all such maps. This invariant measures how widely \(X\) can be spread inside \(Y\) without increasing distances.

A motivating example is the classical sharp theorem that every closed curve of length at most \(4\) in Euclidean space is contained in a closed ball of radius \(1\). If the curve is parametrized by arclength, it is the image of a circle of circumference \(4\) under a nonexpansive map. The theorem can therefore be expressed as a statement about the mapping radius of that metric circle in \(\mathbb{R}^n\). The bound is sharp, as shown by a circle of radius \(1\) in the Euclidean plane.

The work develops a general framework for obtaining such estimates. It studies the behavior of mapping radii under changes in the source and target spaces, including passage to subspaces, products, and convex hulls, and separates those features that depend only on the metric of \(X\) from those arising from the geometry of \(Y\). Particular attention is given to targets that are convex subsets of normed vector spaces, since in that setting centers may be formed by taking convex combinations.

For bounded \(X\), the largest mapping radius obtainable among all convex subsets of normed spaces admits an intrinsic description. For each \(x\in X\), let
\[
d_x(z)=d_X(x,z),\qquad z\in X,
\]
be the distance function associated with \(x\). Then
\[
\sup_{\substack{Y\text{ a convex subset}\\
\text{of a normed space}}}
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,Y)
=
\inf\left\{
\left\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i d_{x_i}\right\|_\infty:
\lambda_i\ge 0,\ 
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i=1
\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, the right-hand side is
\[
\inf_{\mu}
\sup_{z\in X}\int_X d_X(x,z)\,d\mu(x),
\]
where the infimum is taken over finitely supported probability measures on \(X\), or over their appropriate closure when needed. In probabilistic language, one chooses a random point \(x\) of \(X\) so as to minimize the greatest possible expected distance from \(x\) to a fixed point \(z\).

The upper bound follows by taking, for a nonexpansive map \(f:X\to Y\), the convex combination
\[
c=\sum_i\lambda_i f(x_i)
\]
as a candidate center. Convexity and the triangle inequality give
\[
\|f(z)-c\|
\leq
\sum_i\lambda_i\|f(z)-f(x_i)\|
\leq
\sum_i\lambda_i d_X(z,x_i).
\]
Taking the supremum over \(z\), and then the infimum over all convex combinations, yields the desired estimate. A suitable canonical embedding built from the distance functions shows that this bound is optimal when all convex normed targets are allowed.

This characterization turns a geometric extremal problem into a convex optimization problem. For a finite metric space, it becomes a finite linear program: one chooses weights \(\lambda_i\) minimizing
\[
\max_{z\in X}\sum_i\lambda_i d_X(x_i,z).
\]
Consequently, many examples can be calculated explicitly. An interval of length \(L\) has universal convex mapping radius \(L/2\). For an \(n\)-point space in which every two distinct points have distance \(1\), the value is \(1-1/n\), attained by assigning equal weight to all points. For a metric circle of circumference \(L\), the uniform distribution gives a constant average distance \(L/4\), and the resulting value is \(L/4\). Taking \(L=4\) recovers the unit-radius bound for closed curves in Euclidean and, more generally, normed spaces.

The framework also clarifies why diameter alone is often insufficient. Although the elementary estimate
\[
\frac{\operatorname{diam}(X)}{2}
\leq
\sup_Y\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,Y)
\leq
\operatorname{diam}(X)
\]
provides a rough range, the exact value depends on the full configuration of distances in \(X\). Spaces with the same diameter can have substantially different mapping radii because their optimal probability distributions—and hence their best convex centers—may differ.

Beyond these calculations, the theory raises several natural questions. These include determining the mapping radius for important classes of infinite metric spaces, understanding when the infimum is attained by a finite convex combination, comparing the universal convex value with the value for a fixed target such as Euclidean or Hilbert space, and finding efficient structural or algorithmic methods for finite spaces. In this way, mapping radius provides a common language for classical enclosing-ball theorems, Lipschitz mapping problems, convex geometry, and optimization over metric spaces.
outputs.L5:
### Streamlining Property Letting with Digital Tools

Property letting can involve several time-consuming tasks, from advertising a property and screening tenants to collecting rent and arranging maintenance. Fortunately, modern digital tools can make the process more efficient.

Letting agents and landlords can use property management platforms to organize tenancy agreements, monitor payments, and communicate with tenants. Several tools also offer automated reminders, online document signing, and maintenance tracking. By choosing the right solutions, property professionals can reduce administrative work, improve tenant satisfaction, and manage several properties more effectively.

counterfactuals.output:
The article introduces the **mapping radius** of a metric space \(X\) in a metric space \(Y\):
\[
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,Y)
=\sup_{f:X\to Y\ \text{nonexpansive}}
\inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{x\in X} d_Y(f(x),y).
\]
Thus, for every \(1\)-Lipschitz map \(f\), one takes the smallest radius of a ball in \(Y\) containing \(f(X)\), and then maximizes this radius over all such maps.

The paper relates this invariant to familiar quantities such as the diameter and intrinsic radius of \(X\), establishing general inequalities, monotonicity properties, and comparison results for different target spaces. It develops techniques based on embeddings, symmetry, convexity, probability measures, and finite approximations to obtain upper and lower bounds or exact values.

A central result concerns mapping into suitable classes of convex metric or normed spaces. The relevant radius can be characterized through finite convex combinations of distance functions, via an expression of the form
\[
\inf_{\substack{x_1,\dots,x_n\in X\\
\lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_i\lambda_i=1}}
\ \sup_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,d(x,x_i).
\]
This reformulates a geometric mapping problem as a minimax problem involving weighted average distances, connecting mapping radii with ideas related to rendezvous numbers and metric convexity.

Examples illustrate how the invariant behaves for finite metric spaces, highly symmetric spaces, subsets of normed spaces, and various choices of targets. They also show that the answer can depend significantly on whether centers are required to lie in the image, in its convex hull, or anywhere in the ambient target.

The article concludes with open questions about exact computations, optimal target spaces, attainment of the relevant suprema and infima, the role of compactness and convexity, and possible classifications of spaces for which mapping radii coincide with simpler invariants such as half the diameter or the ordinary radius.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft an academic abstract explaining how the classical radius bound for closed curves can be reformulated using the arc-length circle \(S\) and generalized to mappings between metric spaces.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.** Let \(\gamma\) be a rectifiable closed curve of length \(L\). After arc-length parametrization, \(\gamma\) may be regarded as a \(1\)-Lipschitz map from the metric circle \(S_L=\mathbb{R}/L\mathbb{Z}\), equipped with its intrinsic distance, into the ambient space. This reformulation separates the geometry of the parameter space from that of the image. Writing
\[
\operatorname{rad}_Y(f)=\inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{s\in S_L} d_Y\bigl(f(s),y\bigr),
\]
the classical radius estimate becomes
\[
\operatorname{rad}_Y(f)\le \frac{L}{4}\operatorname{Lip}(f),
\]
for normed linear spaces, and more generally for metrically convex targets admitting suitable midpoints. The constant \(1/4\) is sharp, as shown by a segment traversed in both directions. For arbitrary metric targets one retains the universal bound \(L\operatorname{Lip}(f)/2\), while the sharper quarter-length estimate reflects additional convexity of the codomain. This perspective leads naturally to a mapping-radius invariant for metric spaces,
\[
\operatorname{MR}(X,Y)=\sup_{\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le 1}\operatorname{rad}_Y(f),
\]
which extends the radius problem from individual closed curves to general Lipschitz mappings \(f:X\to Y\). The resulting framework clarifies the roles of parametrization, Lipschitz distortion, and target-space convexity, and provides a metric formulation independent of linear or smooth structure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: What is the main result of a paper studying mapping radii in convex subsets of normed metric spaces, especially the formula involving the infimum of sup norms of convex linear combinations of \(d(x,-)\)?
counterfactuals.output:
For a bounded metric space \(X\), the paper’s main result is that its mapping radius over all convex subsets of normed spaces is

\[
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,\mathrm{Conv})
=
\inf_{\substack{n\ge1,\;x_1,\dots,x_n\in X\\
\lambda_i\ge0,\;\sum_i\lambda_i=1}}
\left\|
\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i\,d(x_i,-)
\right\|_\infty .
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,\mathrm{Conv})
=
\inf_{\lambda_i,x_i}
\sup_{x\in X}\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\,d(x_i,x).
\]

Thus, one chooses a finitely supported probability measure on \(X\) and minimizes the largest expected distance from a point \(x\in X\) to a random point drawn from that measure.

The formula is realized through the Kuratowski embedding \(x\mapsto d(x,-)\) into \(\ell^\infty(X)\), taking the convex hull of the embedded copy of \(X\). In this sense, that canonical convex target is universal for computing the mapping radius.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a brief, formal paper abstract on mapping radii that includes the sharp radius-1 bound for curves of length \(\le 4\), theoretical tools for bounded metric spaces, explicit calculations, and open questions.
counterfactuals.output:
We study the mapping radius
\[
\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,Y)=\sup_{f:X\to Y\ \mathrm{1\text{-}Lipschitz}}
\inf_{y\in Y}\sup_{x\in X}d_Y\!\bigl(y,f(x)\bigr)
\]
for bounded metric spaces \(X\) and target spaces \(Y\). Using diameter estimates, admissible-center constructions, injective envelopes, and finite optimization methods, we develop tools for bounding and computing mapping radii. In particular, every closed rectifiable curve of length at most \(4\) mapped nonexpansively into a normed space has image contained in a ball of radius \(1\); the constant is sharp, as shown by a length-\(4\) curve whose image traverses a segment of length \(2\). Explicit calculations are given for intervals, circles, and selected finite metric spaces, including \(\operatorname{map\!-\!rad}(X,\mathbb R)=\tfrac12\operatorname{diam}(X)\). We conclude with open questions concerning extremal targets, attainment of the defining supremum, algorithmic computation for finite spaces, and extensions of the sharp curve bound to broader classes of geodesic and nonlinear target spaces.
